title: Procurement Is Scheduled Backward From the Need Date
summary: Long-lead items such as switchgear, generators, elevators and curtain wall decide the schedule months before the site needs them. Put them on one register, schedule each backward from its need date, expedite with evidence and witness a factory acceptance test before shipment.
body:
Procurement is planned backward from the day each item must be on site. The items that take longest to make, approve and ship decide the schedule long before the site needs them, so they belong on one register, owned by one person, reviewed every week.

Recall

Q. What is an approved fabricator under the building code's special inspection rules?

A. A fabricator recognised by the building official, often through a certification program, whose shop work may be accepted without separate special inspection. Confirm with the official before award.

Q. What does a pre-pour checklist require before concrete is placed?

A. That reinforcement, cover, embedded items and formwork are inspected and accepted, that the curing plan and weather plan are ready, and that the testing agency is booked.

Q. What does life-cycle cost add to a capital cost estimate?

A. Operating, maintenance, replacement and energy costs over the life of the building, usually discounted to present value, so that cheap-to-build but costly-to-run choices are exposed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a building can be perfectly designed, financed and permitted and still open six months late because one electrical switchboard sat in a factory queue. The site cannot build around a missing transformer, a missing elevator or a missing curtain wall. As owner you will not order those items yourself in most delivery methods, but you will pay for every week they are late, so you must be able to read the procurement plan and see the danger early. Quincy leads this week, with Devika on customs and the tax on goods that cross a border.

The long-lead register

In plain English: a list of every item that takes a long time to get, with the date it must arrive and every step between now and then.

A long-lead item is equipment or material whose total time from decision to delivery is long enough to threaten the construction schedule. Typical examples on a building are main electrical switchgear and transformers, emergency generators, elevators, chillers and large air-handling units, fire pumps, curtain wall and windows, structural steel and precast, and specialised fixtures. Lead times move with the market and can stretch dramatically when demand surges, so never rely on last year's number; ask the manufacturer, in writing, now.

The long-lead register is the owner's or contractor's controlled list of those items. For each one it records the specification section, the responsible party, the need date, and a chain of dated steps: design release, bid, award, submittal, approval, release to manufacture, fabrication, testing, shipping, customs, delivery and installation. A second new term: the need date, sometimes called the required-on-site date, is the latest date the item can arrive without delaying the critical path. Everything is scheduled backward from it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. The main switchgear must be on site in week 60 so it can be set, terminated and tested before the utility energises the building. The manufacturer quotes 40 weeks from approved drawings to shipment. Shipping and customs take 6 weeks. Submittal preparation and review take 8 weeks, including one resubmittal. Bid and award take 4 weeks. Working backward from week 60: shipment by week 54, approved drawings by week 14, submittal starts week 6, award by week 6, and bid by week 2. The electrical design for the switchgear must therefore be ready to bid in the second week of the project, which usually means during design development, long before the construction contract exists. If it is not, the owner may need to buy it directly in an early package and assign it to the contractor later.

Say that out loud now.

Expediting and the factory acceptance test

In plain English: once an item is ordered, someone must keep checking that the factory is actually making it, and test it before it ships.

Expediting is the active follow-up of orders: confirming that drawings are approved, materials are bought, the item is in the production slot promised, and shipping is booked. A good expediter does not wait for a missed date; it asks for evidence at each step, such as a photo of the frame on the line or the mill certificate for the steel.

A third new term: the factory acceptance test (FAT), a test of the equipment at the manufacturer's works, witnessed by the buyer or its engineer, before shipment. It checks that the item meets the specification, functions as designed, and carries the certifications the authority will require. A defect found at the factory costs a repair at the factory. The same defect found on site costs a repair, a delay and often a return shipment across an ocean.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A generator fails its witnessed load test at the factory because a control module is faulty. The manufacturer fixes it in 2 weeks and the shipment slips from week 50 to week 52, still inside the week 60 need date. Had the test been skipped and the fault found during site commissioning in week 64, replacement parts would have taken 6 weeks, pushing energisation to week 70. At a hypothetical cost of carry of 100,000 dollars a critical-path week, the witnessed test saved around 1,000,000 dollars.

How the best do it

Leading contractors run procurement as a separate schedule linked into the master schedule, with every long-lead item carrying its own float. They place early equipment packages before the main contract, assign them to the builder, and send their own expediters to the factories of the most critical suppliers. A small developer can copy the principle at small scale: a one-page register, weekly review, written lead-time quotes, and a decision on early purchase of the three or four items most likely to decide the opening date.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: imported equipment may attract customs duty and import value-added or goods and services tax, and who pays depends on the trade term; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: who owns risk in transit must be stated, or a loss at sea becomes a dispute. Banking: lenders may fund deposits on long-lead items only with security. Governance: an owner-purchased early package needs written authority and assignment terms. Estate: none directly. Exit: warranties and factory test records must transfer to a buyer.

Who owns the register

The register only works if one person owns it. On a design-bid-build job that is often the owner's representative until the contractor is appointed, and then the contractor's procurement lead, with the owner's representative auditing it. On a construction management job it may sit with the construction manager from the start. Whoever owns it, the owner should receive it every week in the same format: item, need date, forecast arrival, float, the next step and who must take it. A register that changes shape every month hides trends. A register in the same shape every week shows a float shrinking from ten weeks to six to three long before anyone calls it late, and that early view is the whole point of keeping it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is discovering a long lead time after the construction contract is signed. The control is a long-lead register built during design, with written lead-time quotes and a decision, item by item, on whether the owner buys early.

The beginner's mistake

Scheduling the item from the order date instead of from the need date. The need date is fixed by the critical path; the order date is what you are trying to find.

Callback

Last week, Quincy reverse engineered a steel frame and found that detailing and the mill order had to start four months before erection. Steel is simply one entry on the long-lead register. This week generalises the method to every item that can decide the opening date.

Recap

Build a long-lead register during design. Schedule each item backward from its need date. Get lead times in writing. Expedite with evidence and witness a factory acceptance test before shipment. Decide early which items the owner should buy directly.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the switchgear that arrived and could not be used.
checklist: A long-lead register exists from design development onward.
Every long-lead item has a need date tied to the critical path.
Lead times are quoted in writing by the manufacturer, not assumed.
Each item has a dated chain of steps from design release to installation.
I have decided which items the owner should buy in an early package.
Critical equipment has a witnessed factory acceptance test before shipment.
The register is reviewed every week by a named owner.
head: Field checklist
speak: Procurement is planned backward from the need date: the latest day an item can arrive without delaying the critical path. Long-lead items, like switchgear, transformers, generators, elevators, chillers and curtain wall, can take most of a year from approved drawings to shipment. So I keep a long-lead register, built during design, with a dated chain for each item: design release, bid, award, submittal, approval, manufacture, testing, shipping, customs and delivery. In a hypothetical case, switchgear needed in week 60 with a 40-week factory lead had to be bid in week 2, which meant buying it in an early owner package. Once ordered, an expediter follows each step with evidence, not promises. And before critical equipment ships, I witness a factory acceptance test, because a fault fixed at the factory costs two weeks, while the same fault found on site can cost months and a return shipment.
terms: Long-lead item — equipment or material whose time from decision to delivery is long enough to threaten the schedule.
Need date — the latest date an item can arrive on site without delaying the critical path.
Factory acceptance test — a witnessed test of equipment at the manufacturer's works before it ships.

hostile.q: Your switchgear lead time is 40 weeks and your contractor has not been appointed. How will you meet your energisation date?
hostile.a: By buying it now in an early owner package. The design team is completing the switchgear specification this month, we will bid it to three manufacturers with written lead times, award by week 6, and assign the order to the contractor when it is appointed. The register shows the switchgear with 4 weeks of float to the need date, and we will witness the factory test before it ships.

title: The Switchgear That Arrived and Could Not Be Used
summary: This is a composite example. Cheap imported switchgear shipped on time, was held at the port over its classification and value, and then failed inspection because it lacked the required certification mark. Fifteen weeks of delay cost far more than the saving.
body:
This is a composite example. A new building's main switchgear arrived on time, passed through customs late, and then could not be used, because the local electrical inspector would not accept it without the right certification mark. Every failure in the chain was a procurement failure, not an electrical one.

Recall

Q. What is a need date?

A. The latest date an item can arrive on site without delaying the critical path. Long-lead items are scheduled backward from it.

Q. What does Rule 114 require?

A. No change to a load path is fabricated until a named engineer has recalculated it and signed the result; a stamp without a calculation is not a check.

Q. What is the in-balance test in a construction loan?

A. Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the full cost to complete before the lender advances another draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous procurement failures are the quiet ones: a missing label, a wrong classification code, a test nobody witnessed. They cost little to prevent and a great deal to repair. Ford takes this composite case through seven steps, and Cole assists on customs and the legal duties that sit behind the paperwork.

1. Timeline

A hypothetical mid-size building. In design, the electrical engineer specified main switchgear and a large transformer. To save money, the contractor bought both from an overseas manufacturer with no local track record. The order was placed late, with a quoted 30-week lead. The factory shipped on time on a trade term that made the buyer responsible from the factory's door. The goods were held at the port for 5 weeks after customs questioned the classification and the declared value. When the switchgear reached site, the electrical inspector refused to approve it because it did not carry the certification mark from a nationally recognised testing laboratory that the local electrical code required. Field certification took a further 10 weeks. Energisation slipped by about 15 weeks.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the outcome. Buying from a manufacturer that had never supplied the market. Accepting a trade term that put transit risk and customs responsibility on the buyer without a broker briefed in advance. And omitting a witnessed factory acceptance test because the price was already tight.

3. Assumptions

The team assumed that equipment built to an international standard would be accepted locally. It assumed that customs clearance was routine. It assumed that the supplier's own test certificate was as good as a witnessed test. Each assumption was reasonable on its face and none was checked. In American practice, electrical equipment is generally required to be listed or labelled by a recognised testing organisation for the use intended [unverified — confirm independently], and the authority having jurisdiction decides what it will accept. That question belonged in the bid documents.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

The contractor's buyer was rewarded for the lowest price, not the lowest total cost. The manufacturer was rewarded for shipping on time, which it did. The freight forwarder was paid to move a box, not to understand what was in it. Nobody's incentive covered the gap between the factory door and a switchboard the inspector would sign off. Cole's point: when no party is paid to own a gap, the owner owns it by default.

5. Warning signs ignored

The submittal arrived without the certification mark shown on the nameplate drawing, and the engineer noted it as a comment rather than a rejection. The manufacturer asked twice for the exact classification code the buyer wanted declared, and the request went unanswered. The commercial invoice showed a lower value than the purchase order. Each sign was small. Together they said that nobody had planned the arrival.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was shipment without certification. Before shipment, the factory could have applied the required mark through its testing laboratory or the team could have arranged a witnessed test. After shipment, the only path was field evaluation of equipment already installed, done on the laboratory's schedule, while the building sat without permanent power.

7. Root cause

The root cause was that procurement was treated as purchasing a price rather than delivering a usable, accepted item to a need date. The specification did not require the local certification, the long-lead register did not include customs and approval steps, and no single person owned the item from design to energisation.

Cole's view: the paperwork has legal weight

A customs declaration is the importer's statement of what the goods are, where they come from and what they are worth. In most countries the importer of record is responsible for its accuracy, and errors in classification or value can bring penalties, delays, and in serious cases investigation, even when the error was a supplier's. A commercial invoice that shows a value different from the real price is not a clerical issue; it is the kind of discrepancy customs is trained to find. Verify the rules in your jurisdiction against the primary source before you rely on them. Professional sign-off required: a licensed customs broker for classification and declarations, and a lawyer if any discrepancy has already been filed.

A worked example of the cost

Hypothetical figures. The overseas switchgear saved 150,000 dollars against a local quote. The delays cost 15 critical-path weeks at a cost of carry of 90,000 dollars a week, which is 1,350,000 dollars, plus 60,000 dollars of field certification, 25,000 dollars of port storage and demurrage, and temporary generator power at 8,000 dollars a week for 15 weeks, 120,000 dollars. Total cost of the saving: about 1,555,000 dollars, more than ten times what was saved.

What a prevention plan looks like

Run the same case again with controls in place. During design, the electrical engineer writes the local certification requirement into the specification, and the owner's representative confirms with the authority having jurisdiction that it will accept that mark. The long-lead register carries the switchgear with steps for submittal, certification, factory test, export, customs, delivery and inspection, each with a date and owner. The bid documents ask every manufacturer to state, in its bid, the certification it will apply and its experience in the market. A licensed customs broker receives the technical data at award and agrees the classification in writing with the importer. The purchase order makes shipment release conditional on a passed witnessed test and on the certification mark being applied at the works. With those six steps, the cheaper overseas supplier might still have won, and the project would have kept the saving. The point is not to avoid imports. It is to buy the whole chain, not just the box.

Notice that none of these steps needs special expertise from the owner. Each one needs a question asked at the right moment and an answer written down. Ford's point is that most procurement failures are failures of timing: the right question asked after shipment is worthless.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating the factory door as the finish line. The control is to write the whole chain, from design release through certification, customs and inspector acceptance, into the register and the purchase order, with a named owner for every step.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a supplier's certificate equals local acceptance. The authority having jurisdiction decides what it will accept, and the bid documents must ask that question first.

Callback

In Week 72, REGA and Cole taught that integrity rules, such as accurate declarations and knowing who you deal with, protect reputation as much as they prevent penalties. A falsely low customs value saves a little duty and buys a lasting record with the customs authority, which follows the importer into every future shipment.

Recap

Cheap switchgear arrived on time, sat at the port, and then failed inspection for lack of a required certification mark. Fifteen weeks of delay cost ten times the saving. Rule 115 makes acceptance, not shipment, the definition of delivered.

Next: Nadia on The Money: landed cost, payment terms and the price of buying from abroad.
checklist: The specification requires the certification the local authority will accept.
I have asked the authority having jurisdiction about acceptance before bid.
The long-lead register includes certification, customs and inspection steps.
A licensed customs broker has the classification and documents before shipment.
The commercial invoice value matches the purchase order.
Critical equipment has a witnessed factory acceptance test.
One named person owns each long-lead item from design to acceptance.
A submittal missing a required mark is rejected, not noted.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A contractor saved 150,000 dollars buying switchgear from an overseas manufacturer new to the market. It shipped on time, on a term that made the buyer responsible from the factory door. Customs held it for five weeks over its classification and a commercial invoice value that did not match the order. Then the electrical inspector refused it, because it lacked the certification mark the local code required, and field certification took ten more weeks. Energisation slipped fifteen weeks, and the total cost was more than ten times the saving. The root cause was treating procurement as buying a price, not delivering an accepted item to a need date. The warning signs were all on paper: a submittal without the mark, unanswered questions about classification, and a mismatched invoice. My rule: an item is delivered only when it is on site, cleared, certified and accepted by the inspector.
terms: Authority having jurisdiction — the official or body with legal power to approve equipment, installations and buildings.
Importer of record — the party legally responsible for a shipment's customs declaration and duties.
Listed or labelled equipment — equipment certified by a recognised testing organisation for a stated use.

hostile.q: Your contractor saved 150,000 dollars on switchgear. Why are you insisting on a local certification and a witnessed test that wipe out half the saving?
hostile.a: Because the saving is not real until the inspector accepts the equipment. If it arrives without the certification our authority requires, field evaluation and delay can cost ten times the saving. I will keep the overseas supplier if it can apply the required mark at the factory and pass a witnessed test before shipment; if it cannot, the local quote is the cheaper one.

rule: Rule 115: An item is not delivered until it is on site, cleared, certified and accepted by the authority; specify, register and test for acceptance, not for shipment.

title: Landed Cost: What an Imported Item Really Costs
summary: A supplier's quote is only the start. Landed cost adds packing, freight, insurance, duty, import tax, brokerage, port and inland charges, and the cost of currency movement and early payment. Compare suppliers on landed cost, not quoted price.
body:
The price on a supplier's quote is not what an imported item costs you. Landed cost adds packing, freight, insurance, duty, import tax, brokerage, port and inland charges, currency movement and the cost of paying early, and on some items those extras decide which supplier is really cheapest.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a deposit increase from a late fabricator?

A. Whether the fabricator is short of cash. An extra deposit to a struggling shop is an unsecured loan, so it should be secured by marked goods or a bond.

Q. Why is curing concrete a cost item and not just a site habit?

A. Poor curing lowers strength and durability, causing low breaks, coring, repairs and possibly removal, so the curing plan protects money already spent.

Q. What is the difference between first cost and life-cycle cost?

A. First cost is the price to build or buy. Life-cycle cost adds operating, maintenance, energy and replacement costs over the asset's life, usually discounted to present value.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you build in a market that imports most of its equipment and finishes, the gap between quoted price and landed cost can be large, and it is often where a budget quietly fails. Nadia teaches you to build landed cost line by line, to see the currency exposure, and to price the cash you hand over before anything arrives.

Building landed cost

In plain English: landed cost is everything you pay to get the item to your site, cleared and ready to install.

The professional framing is a stack, built in order: the supplier's price at its own premises, export packing and loading, main freight, cargo insurance, customs duty, import value-added tax or goods and services tax where it applies, customs brokerage, port and terminal charges, inland transport to site, and any storage. Which of those you pay directly depends on the trade term in the contract, which Devika covers tomorrow. Whoever pays them, the project bears them in the end.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. Two hundred windows are quoted at 400,000 dollars at the factory. Export packing is 8,000 dollars. Sea freight is 30,000 dollars. Cargo insurance is 4,000 dollars. Customs duty, at a hypothetical rate of 10 percent on a customs value of 442,000 dollars, the goods plus freight and insurance, is 44,200 dollars. Some countries value goods on that basis and some exclude the international freight, which is one more reason to let a broker set the figure. The real rate depends on the classification and the country; this one is for illustration only. Brokerage is 2,000 dollars, port charges 3,000 dollars and inland trucking 6,000 dollars. Landed cost before import tax: 400,000 plus 8,000, 30,000, 4,000, 44,200, 2,000, 3,000 and 6,000 is 497,200 dollars. The extras add about 24 percent to the quoted price. A local supplier quoting 470,000 dollars delivered is now the cheaper option, though its quote looked 70,000 dollars higher.

Import value-added tax or goods and services tax adds a further layer. If the project is registered and can recover that tax as an input credit, it is mainly a cash-flow cost: you pay it at the border and recover it later. If it cannot recover it, it is a real cost. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say that out loud now.

Currency: the price that moves after you agree it

In plain English: if the supplier prices in a currency other than the one you borrow and earn in, the price can change after you sign.

A new term: currency exposure, the amount of a future payment whose value in your own currency depends on the exchange rate. Suppose the windows are priced at 360,000 euros, converted today at a hypothetical 1.10 dollars per euro, which is 396,000 dollars. Balance is paid in 6 months. If the euro rises to 1.20, the same 360,000 euros cost 432,000 dollars, 36,000 dollars more. You can carry the risk, ask for pricing in your own currency, or buy a forward contract, an agreement to exchange currency at a fixed rate on a future date. Week 43 taught the instruments. Here the point is to see the exposure and decide. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any hedging product.

Paying early has a price

Overseas suppliers commonly ask for a deposit on order and the balance against shipping documents, often through a letter of credit, a bank's promise to pay on presentation of specified documents. These are commercial practices, negotiated each time. The money paid before delivery has a cost: interest on the borrowed funds, or the return your equity could have earned elsewhere.

A second worked example, hypothetical. On the 400,000 dollar window order, 30 percent, 120,000 dollars, is paid on order, 10 months before installation. The balance of 280,000 dollars is paid against documents, 3 months before installation. At an 8 percent annual cost of capital, the deposit costs 120,000 times 8 percent times 10 over 12, which is 8,000 dollars, and the balance costs 280,000 times 8 percent times 3 over 12, which is 5,600 dollars. The letter of credit adds a hypothetical bank fee of 0.5 percent of the 280,000 dollars, 1,400 dollars. Early payment adds about 15,000 dollars to the true cost. Small against the order, but it belongs in the comparison, and it grows quickly if the item arrives late and sits paid for and idle.

Storage and the cost of arriving early

An item that arrives well before its need date is not free safety. It needs secure storage, insurance, protection from humidity and salt air, and sometimes periodic maintenance, such as rotating a motor shaft. Early arrival also starts some warranty periods before the building opens. A planner aims for a deliberate buffer, not maximum earliness.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On a personal balance sheet, an open foreign-currency purchase commitment is a liability whose size you do not yet know. If your project equity is in one currency and a large share of its cost is in another, your net worth moves with the exchange rate whether or not you look. Write the exposure down, at today's rate and at a stressed rate, and decide deliberately whether to carry it.

Putting it on one page

Nadia's landed-cost sheet has the same rows for every bid: quoted price and its currency, exchange rate used and a stressed rate, packing, freight, insurance, broker's duty estimate with the classification code, import tax and whether it is recoverable, brokerage, port, inland, storage, deposit and letter-of-credit cost, and total. One column per supplier. The sheet forces every bidder's number onto the same basis, and it makes the conversation with the contractor's buyer short: the cheapest supplier is the one with the lowest total on the bottom row, after the stressed currency line.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing suppliers on quoted price rather than landed cost. The control is a standard landed-cost sheet, completed for every imported bid, including currency at a stressed rate and the cost of early payment.

The beginner's mistake

Treating import tax as always recoverable. Whether it is a cash-flow cost or a real cost depends on registration and the use of the building, and must be checked.

Callback

In Week 62, Devika taught that indirect taxes such as value-added and goods and services tax can be either a timing cost or a real cost depending on recovery. Landed cost is where that distinction becomes money: the same tax can be a three-month loan to the government or a permanent cost of the building.

Recap

Landed cost stacks freight, insurance, duty, tax, brokerage, port and inland charges on the quoted price. Foreign-currency pricing adds exposure that can be carried, shifted or hedged. Early payment and early arrival both cost money. Compare suppliers only on landed cost.

Next: Devika on The Rules: trade terms, customs classification and the tax on imported goods, with a two-systems comparison.
checklist: Every imported bid has a completed landed-cost sheet.
Customs duty is estimated from a broker's classification, not a guess.
I know whether import tax is recoverable for this project.
Foreign-currency exposure is shown at today's rate and a stressed rate.
The cost of deposits and letters of credit is included in the comparison.
Early arrival has a storage, insurance and protection plan.
I compare local and imported options on landed, not quoted, cost.
head: Field checklist
speak: The quoted price of an imported item is not its cost. Landed cost stacks export packing, freight, insurance, customs duty, brokerage, port charges and inland trucking on top, and in a hypothetical window order those extras added about a quarter, so a local supplier that looked more expensive was cheaper. Import value-added or goods and services tax is a cash-flow cost if the project can recover it and a real cost if it cannot, so I check. If the price is in another currency, the cost moves after I sign; a ten percent move on a large order is real money, so I decide whether to carry it, shift it or hedge it with advice. Deposits and letters of credit cost interest and fees, and early arrival costs storage and protection. So every imported bid gets a landed-cost sheet, with currency stressed, before I compare suppliers.
terms: Landed cost — the full cost of an item delivered to site and cleared, including freight, insurance, duty, taxes and charges.
Currency exposure — the part of a future payment whose value in your own currency depends on the exchange rate.
Forward contract — an agreement to exchange currencies at a fixed rate on a future date.

hostile.q: Your imported windows are 70,000 dollars cheaper than the local bid. Why are you recommending the local supplier?
hostile.a: Because on landed cost they are not cheaper. Freight, insurance, a broker's estimate of duty, port and inland charges add about 97,000 dollars, before currency risk on a euro price and the interest on a 30 percent deposit. On a like-for-like delivered basis, the local bid is about 27,000 dollars lower, with less currency and delivery risk. The sheet is attached line by line.

title: Trade Terms, Classification and the Border
summary: Incoterms 2020 decide who pays each leg, who bears risk and who clears customs, but not who owns the goods. Classification, customs value and origin decide duty and import tax. Canada and Guyana both treat the importer's declaration as a legal statement and grant concessions by process.
body:
Every cross-border purchase answers three questions: who pays for each leg of the journey, who bears the risk if the goods are lost or damaged, and who clears them through customs. A trade term in the contract answers all three, and the customs classification decides what the border will charge.

Recall

Q. What is landed cost?

A. The full cost of an item delivered to site and cleared, including the supplier's price, packing, freight, insurance, duty, import tax, brokerage, port charges and inland transport.

Q. What records should a steel frame's compliance file contain?

A. Mill test reports, welding procedures and welder qualifications, bolt lot certificates, special inspection reports and, where the fabricator is approved, its certificate of compliance.

Q. What does a value engineering proposal need to show besides first-cost saving?

A. Its effect on life-cycle cost, performance, durability and maintenance, so that a cheaper item is not a costlier building.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a purchase order with the wrong trade term can leave you paying for goods lost at sea, or paying duty you thought the supplier had paid. Customs rules are strict about classification, value and origin, and the importer usually carries the liability for mistakes. Devika teaches the frame so you can read a quote and know where your risk begins.

Trade terms: Incoterms 2020

In plain English: a three-letter code in the contract says where the seller's job ends and the buyer's begins.

The professional framing is Incoterms, the International Chamber of Commerce's standard trade terms, of which the current version is Incoterms 2020. There are 11 rules. Some can be used for any mode of transport, including the ones most used for project equipment: EXW, ex works, where the buyer does almost everything from the seller's premises; FCA, free carrier, where the seller hands over to the buyer's carrier, export cleared; CPT and CIP, carriage paid to, and carriage and insurance paid to, where the seller pays main carriage to a named place; DAP, delivered at place; DPU, delivered at place unloaded; and DDP, delivered duty paid, where the seller delivers, cleared for import with duties paid. Four are for sea and inland waterway only: FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF. Verify the current rules against the official text before you rely on them.

The trap is that cost and risk do not always move together. Under CIF, cost, insurance and freight, the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port, but risk passes to the buyer once the goods are loaded on board at origin. If the ship is damaged at sea, the buyer bears the loss and claims on the insurance. Incoterms also do not decide when title passes. That is a matter for the sales contract and the governing law.

A worked example. A chiller is bought CIF a destination port at a hypothetical 600,000 dollars. A crane drops it while unloading at destination. Risk passed at loading at origin, so the loss is the buyer's, recoverable from the cargo insurance only if the policy covers unloading and the claim is made on time. The insurance the seller must buy under CIF is minimum cover unless the contract asks for more, so the buyer should specify the cover it needs.

Say that out loud now.

Customs classification, value and origin

In plain English: the border wants to know what the goods are, what they are worth and where they were made, and each answer changes the bill.

A new term: tariff classification, the code assigned to goods under the Harmonized System, an international nomenclature maintained by the World Customs Organization and used by most countries as the base of their tariffs. The code decides the duty rate. Customs value is usually the transaction value, the price actually paid or payable, adjusted for certain items such as assists or royalties, under rules most countries draw from the World Trade Organization's valuation agreement. Origin decides whether a trade agreement's preferential rate applies, and claiming it usually needs a valid certificate or declaration of origin. Professional sign-off required: a licensed customs broker on classification, value and origin.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A packaged air-handling unit could be classified as a single machine or as its separate parts. Suppose one classification carries a hypothetical 5 percent duty and the other 15 percent. On a 300,000 dollar customs value, that is 15,000 dollars against 45,000 dollars. The difference is real, but the correct answer is whichever classification the rules require, not the cheaper one. A wrong classification chosen to save duty is a false declaration.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is an odd week, so Devika compares how the two countries approach imports, conceptually. Verify everything here against the primary source before you rely on it.

In Canada, imports are administered by the Canada Border Services Agency under a federal customs tariff built on the Harmonized System. Goods and services tax, and in some provinces the harmonized sales tax, is generally collected on imports at the border, and a registered business can usually claim it back as an input tax credit when it is used in taxable activity. Canada's trade agreements, such as the agreement with the United States and Mexico, can lower duty on goods that qualify by origin.

In Guyana, customs and the value-added tax on imports are administered by the Guyana Revenue Authority. As a member of the Caribbean Community, Guyana applies a common external tariff to many goods from outside the community, and goods of community origin may enter on preferential terms. Investment regimes may offer duty or tax concessions on approved project imports, usually through an application and approval process with conditions attached.

The shared lesson: in both systems the importer's declaration is a legal statement, classification and origin decide the bill, and concessions are granted by process, not assumed.

Who owns the goods in transit

Because Incoterms do not settle title, the purchase order should. In the United States, sales of goods are governed by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code as enacted in each state, and international sales between parties in different countries may fall under the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods unless the contract excludes it. Verify which applies against the primary source. Professional sign-off required: a construction or trade lawyer on governing law, title and risk.

A second look at DDP and EXW

The two ends of the Incoterms range teach the most. Under EXW the buyer collects from the seller's premises and handles export clearance in the seller's country, which a foreign buyer may not legally be able to do, so FCA is often the better choice. Under DDP the seller handles import clearance and pays duty in the buyer's country, which a foreign seller may not be registered to do. Both extremes ask a party to act in a country where it may have no standing. The middle terms, where each side clears its own border, are usually the practical ones for project equipment.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a trade term by habit and discovering after a loss that risk passed long before cost did. The control is to choose the term deliberately, name the place precisely, specify the insurance cover, and state title separately in the purchase order.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking DDP removes all import risk. Under DDP the seller must be able to act as importer in your country; if it cannot, the shipment stalls, and some buyers then become importer of record without planning to.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught that substance beats form and that penalties follow false statements. A customs declaration is a statement of fact about goods. Choosing a classification for its rate rather than its accuracy is the trade-goods version of the avoidance-versus-evasion line.

Recap

Incoterms 2020 split cost, risk and clearance between seller and buyer, but not title. Classification, value and origin decide duty. Canada and Guyana both treat the importer's declaration as a legal statement and grant concessions by process. State title and insurance in the purchase order.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: building a procurement chain with float and pricing the cost of expediting.
checklist: Every import purchase order names an Incoterms 2020 rule and a precise place.
I know where risk passes and where cost passes, and they may differ.
The cargo insurance cover is specified, not left at the minimum.
Title is stated separately in the purchase order.
A licensed customs broker confirms classification, value and origin before shipment.
Preferential origin claims have valid documents.
Any duty concession is applied for and approved, not assumed.
Governing law for the sale is stated and reviewed by a lawyer.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every import answers three questions: who pays each leg, who carries the risk, and who clears customs. Incoterms 2020, the International Chamber of Commerce's eleven trade terms, answer them. The trap is that cost and risk can split: under CIF the seller pays freight and insurance to my port, but the risk becomes mine once the goods are loaded at origin. Incoterms also say nothing about title, so the purchase order must. At the border, three facts set the bill: the Harmonized System classification, the customs value, usually the price paid, and the origin, which can unlock a lower rate. The importer's declaration is a legal statement, so a licensed broker confirms it. Canada and Guyana both work this way in concept: Canada through its border agency with goods and services tax on imports, Guyana through its revenue authority within the Caribbean Community tariff, with concessions granted only by approval.
terms: Incoterms 2020 — the International Chamber of Commerce's standard trade terms allocating cost, risk and customs duties between seller and buyer.
Tariff classification — the Harmonized System code assigned to goods, which sets the duty rate.
Customs value — the value on which duty is assessed, usually the transaction value of the goods.

hostile.q: You bought the chiller CIF and it was dropped at our port. Why should the supplier not pay?
hostile.a: Under CIF, risk passed to us when the chiller was loaded at origin, even though the supplier paid the freight. So the claim is on the cargo insurance. We specified extended cover in the purchase order, including unloading at destination, and we have notified the insurer within the policy period. I will send you the survey report and the claim timetable.

title: Float on a Procurement Chain, and What Recovery Costs
summary: Add up every step of a long-lead item's chain, compare the arrival with the need date, and the difference is its float. When a delay eats the float, price each recovery option, such as air freight, pre-clearance or resequencing, against the cost of a critical-path week.
body:
A procurement chain is a small schedule of its own. Add up its steps, compare the result with the need date, and you get the item's float; when the float runs out, price the options to recover it against what a critical-path week costs.

Recall

Q. Under CIF, when does risk pass to the buyer?

A. When the goods are loaded on board the vessel at the port of origin, even though the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port.

Q. What does Rule 114 require for a connection change?

A. That a named engineer recalculates it and signs the result before anything is fabricated.

Q. Why is first cost a poor basis for choosing building equipment on its own?

A. Because energy, maintenance and replacement over the equipment's life can exceed its purchase price, so life-cycle cost is the fairer comparison.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a supplier says an item is running late, the only useful response is a number: how many weeks of float does the item have left, and what does each recovery option cost? This is an odd week, so Quincy works forward, step by step, from design release to installation, with hypothetical round numbers.

Step 1: list the chain

The item is a water-cooled chiller. Its need date, set by the commissioning schedule, is week 70 of the project. Quincy lists every step and its duration in weeks. Design release of the final specification: done in week 10. Bid and evaluation: 3 weeks. Award and order: 1 week. Submittal preparation by the manufacturer: 3 weeks. Engineer's review: 2 weeks. One resubmittal and review: 2 weeks. Release to manufacture and factory lead time: 30 weeks. Factory acceptance test, witnessed: 1 week. Inland transport to port and export clearance: 1 week. Sea freight: 4 weeks. Customs clearance and port handling: 2 weeks. Inland delivery to site: 1 week.

Step 2: add it up

Start at week 10. Add 3 for bid, 1 for award, 3 for submittal, 2 for review and 2 for resubmittal: week 21, approved drawings. Add 30 for manufacture: week 51. Add 1 for the factory test: week 52. Add 1 for export, 4 for freight, 2 for customs and 1 for delivery: week 60. The chiller arrives on site in week 60.

Step 3: compute the float

The need date is week 70 and the forecast arrival is week 60. The float is 10 weeks. That is the item's buffer: it can absorb up to 10 weeks of delay in its chain before it delays the critical path. Quincy records that float on the long-lead register and watches it every week. Float is consumed silently; a review that runs 3 weeks instead of 2 has used a week whether or not anyone mentions it.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: a delay arrives

In week 45, the manufacturer reports that a compressor component is late and the factory lead time will grow by 12 weeks. New arrival: week 72. The float was 10 weeks, so the item is now 2 weeks late against its need date, and because commissioning is on the critical path, the project finish moves by 2 weeks unless something is done.

Step 5: price the recovery options

At a hypothetical cost of carry of 90,000 dollars a critical-path week, doing nothing costs 2 weeks, which is 180,000 dollars. Quincy prices three options.

Option A, air freight instead of sea. It saves 3 weeks of sea freight, since air takes about a week instead of four. That brings arrival from week 72 to week 69, one week ahead of the need date. The hypothetical premium for air freight on a large chiller is 120,000 dollars. Cost 120,000 dollars, saving 180,000 dollars of delay. Net benefit 60,000 dollars, with one week of float restored.

Option B, pre-clearance. The broker files the customs entry before arrival and the chiller moves straight to a waiting truck, saving 1 week of the 2 allowed for customs. Cost 5,000 dollars in extra broker time. Saves 1 week, 90,000 dollars, but leaves the item still 1 week late on its own.

Option C, resequence commissioning. The commissioning authority tests the cooling towers, pumps and controls before the chiller arrives, then commissions the chiller last. This takes 2 weeks of chiller-dependent work off the critical path at a cost of 20,000 dollars in extra coordination. It does not move the arrival but removes the 2 weeks of impact.

Best combination: Options B and C together cost 25,000 dollars and fully absorb the delay, leaving 1 week of float. Option A is kept in reserve if the factory slips again. The lesson is that the cheapest recovery is often in the logic, not in the freight.

A second worked example: expediting a submittal

On a second item, a set of elevators, the factory slot depends on approved drawings by week 24. The architect's review is forecast to finish in week 26. Each week of lost factory slot costs 2 weeks at the end, because the manufacturer's next production slot is a fortnight later. Paying the architect's team a hypothetical 15,000 dollars in overtime to finish the review in week 24 protects 4 weeks of finish date, worth 360,000 dollars at 90,000 dollars a week. Expediting a review is often the highest-return dollar in the whole procurement plan.

Step 6: what the register should show after the decision

Once the recovery is chosen, the register changes in four places. The chiller's forecast arrival moves to week 71 with pre-clearance, the need date for chiller-dependent commissioning moves to week 72 because of the resequencing, the float is recorded as 1 week, and the reserve option, air freight at 120,000 dollars, is noted with its own decision date: the day the factory confirms completion. The cost of the chosen recovery, 25,000 dollars, is recorded against the project contingency with the reason. That record matters later. If the supplier's delay turns out to be its fault under the purchase order, the 25,000 dollars may be recoverable, and the claim is only as good as the dated record of what was done and why.

The habit behind the numbers

Quincy's habit is to run this calculation before the delay arrives. For each of the five most critical items, he writes down in advance what he would do if the float fell to four weeks, to two weeks and to zero, and what each step would cost. When a supplier rings with bad news, the answer is already priced, and the conversation is about which prepared option to use, not about what to do. Practitioners find that prepared options are decided in a day, while unprepared ones take weeks, and those weeks come out of the very float they were meant to protect.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is float that nobody tracks until it is gone. The control is a long-lead register that shows each item's remaining float every week, with an agreed trigger, for example 4 weeks of float, at which recovery options must be priced and decided.

The beginner's mistake

Reaching for air freight first. Freight is the most visible lever and often the most expensive; the logic of the schedule and the speed of reviews are usually cheaper.

Callback

In Week 80, Roman taught the risk register with owners and triggers, drawing on N-1 contingency thinking from grid operations: plan for the loss of any single element. The long-lead register applies the same idea to supply. Each critical item should have a known float, a trigger, and a prepared recovery option before it is needed.

Recap

List the chain, add it up, compare with the need date to find float, and watch float every week. When a delay arrives, price each recovery option against the cost of a critical-path week. Logic changes and faster reviews often beat freight.

Next: Quincy on The Room: the factory acceptance test that fails, and the supplier who wants to ship anyway.
checklist: Every long-lead item's chain is listed step by step with durations.
Forecast arrival is compared with the need date to give float.
Remaining float is reported on the register every week.
A float trigger forces recovery options to be priced and decided.
Recovery options are priced against the cost of a critical-path week.
Schedule logic and review speed are tested before paying for faster freight.
A reserve recovery option is identified for each critical item.
head: Field checklist
speak: A procurement chain is a small schedule. For a hypothetical chiller I list every step: bid, award, submittal, review, a resubmittal, a 30-week factory lead, a witnessed factory test, export, sea freight, customs and delivery. Adding them up from week 10 gives arrival in week 60. The need date is week 70, so the float is 10 weeks. I watch that float every week, because it disappears quietly. When the factory reports a 12-week slip, the chiller is 2 weeks late, worth 180,000 dollars at our cost of carry. Air freight would fix it for 120,000 dollars. But pre-clearing customs and resequencing commissioning, testing pumps, towers and controls before the chiller arrives, fix it for 25,000 dollars and keep air freight in reserve. The cheapest recovery is often in the schedule logic and in faster reviews, not in the freight.
terms: Float — the amount of time an activity or item can slip without delaying the critical path or its need date.
Pre-clearance — filing customs entries before goods arrive so they can be released on arrival.
Float trigger — an agreed level of remaining float at which recovery options must be priced and decided.

hostile.q: The chiller is now two weeks late. Why are you not paying for air freight immediately?
hostile.a: Because there is a cheaper fix. Pre-clearing customs saves a week for about 5,000 dollars, and resequencing commissioning so the pumps, towers and controls are tested first takes the chiller off the critical path for about 20,000 dollars. Together they absorb the delay for 25,000 dollars against 120,000 for air freight. If the factory slips again, air freight is already priced and ready.

title: The Factory Test Fails and the Supplier Wants to Ship
summary: A chiller fails its witnessed performance test and the supplier offers to ship and fix it on site. Ask for the cause and a retest at the works, check the float before reacting to the vessel booking, keep payment tied to a passed test, and confirm everything in writing the same day.
body:
When equipment fails its factory acceptance test, the supplier will often offer to ship it anyway and fix it on site. The right answer is usually no, and the skill is saying no in a way that keeps the supplier working for you.

Recall

Q. What is float on a procurement chain?

A. The difference between the item's forecast arrival and its need date: the delay it can absorb before it delays the critical path.

Q. What is the difference between cost and risk under an Incoterms rule?

A. Cost is who pays for each leg; risk is who bears loss or damage. They can pass at different points, as under CIF.

Q. What is the cost of carry used for in decisions about speed?

A. It prices a critical-path week, as interest, general conditions and forgone income, so that any option to save time can be compared with its premium.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a failed factory test arrives with time pressure built in. The supplier has a ship booked, your schedule has a need date, and everyone in the meeting would like the problem to go away. Quincy shows you how to hold the line on quality without wrecking the relationship.

The scene

Week 50 of a hypothetical job. A video call from the manufacturer's works overseas. Present: you, your mechanical engineer who witnessed the test, the contractor's procurement manager, and the manufacturer's sales director. The chiller passed its pressure test but failed its performance test: at full load it delivered about 8 percent less cooling than specified and its efficiency was below the guaranteed figure. The sales director says the shortfall is a calibration issue, that a technician will correct it during site commissioning, and that delaying shipment will cost the vessel booking and three weeks.

The question behind the question

The question behind the request is who will carry the risk if the fix does not work. Once the chiller ships, payment against shipping documents usually becomes due, your leverage falls, and any remedy happens on your site, on your schedule and in your building. A fault the supplier calls calibration might be a compressor or heat exchanger problem that cannot be fixed in the field. Their confidence is not evidence.

The lines to say

"Thank you for running the test properly and showing us the result. That is exactly why we witness."

"Before we talk about shipping, I need to understand the cause. What specifically will the technician change, and can you make that change and rerun the performance test at the works this week?"

"If the retest passes, we ship. If you need more time, let us look at the vessel options together now."

"If we did agree to ship with an open defect, what security would you offer: retention of part of the price, an extended warranty, and a written commitment to replace the unit if the site test fails?"

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

"Just ship it, we will sort it out on site." This moves the whole risk to you.

"The test was probably too strict." It invites the supplier to argue the specification instead of fixing the unit.

"Our schedule cannot take any delay." It tells the supplier that time is your weakness and quality is negotiable.

When to stay silent

After you ask whether they can make the change and retest at the works this week, wait. The sales director will often look to the factory engineer. What the engineer says, or does not say, is the most reliable signal in the call about whether this is really calibration.

Holding your state

A failed test feels like a crisis, but it is the system working. Remind yourself that the factory test exists so that this conversation happens now, at the works, rather than in six months in a plant room. Slow down, speak in short sentences, and let your engineer give the technical facts. Your role is to set the conditions.

A worked example of the decision

The factory says it can adjust and retest in 5 days, missing the booked vessel; the next vessel is 9 days later. Quincy checks the register: the chiller had 10 weeks of float before this week's events and still has 7. A 9-day slip costs about 1.3 weeks of float and nothing on the critical path. Shipping a unit that underperforms by 8 percent would, at worst, mean a replacement that takes 30 weeks, far beyond the float, at a hypothetical cost of carry of 90,000 dollars a week. The decision is not close: retest at the works.

A second check, the money. The order is 600,000 dollars, with 70 percent due against shipping documents. Holding shipment keeps 420,000 dollars in your hands until the unit passes, which is the strongest incentive you have for the factory to put its best engineer on the problem.

After the call: what goes in writing

Quincy sends a short note the same day. The test result and the specified values. The supplier's agreed action and retest date. The statement that shipment will not be released until the performance test passes, witnessed. The effect on the long-lead register: float reduced from 7 weeks to about 5.7. And a request for the supplier's root-cause explanation in writing. A clear written record protects the relationship, because nobody has to remember who promised what.

The relationship after the no

A supplier who has been told no in the right way usually works harder, not less. The no was about the unit, not about the company, it came with a clear path to yes, and it came with a written record that protects the supplier too: if the site later finds a different problem, nobody can claim the factory hid this one. Quincy ends calls like this with a specific thank-you to the factory engineer for the test data. That engineer is the person who will be on the phone at two in the morning during commissioning, and the relationship is built now.

When shipping with an open defect is acceptable

Sometimes it is. If the defect is minor, cosmetic or clearly fixable in the field with parts that ship with the unit, and the float is already gone, an owner may accept shipment with conditions: part of the price retained until the site test passes, an extended warranty on the affected component, the supplier's technician on site at its cost, and a written commitment to replace the unit if the site performance test fails. Those conditions turn a promise into a contract term. Professional sign-off required: your mechanical engineer on whether the defect is genuinely field-fixable, and your lawyer on the wording of the conditions.

The note for the lender

If a lender's monitor is watching the project, tell it the same day. A short note saying the chiller failed its factory test, that shipment is held pending a retest, and that the register shows float remaining, is far better than the monitor finding a slipped delivery in next month's report. Lenders forgive problems that arrive with a plan. They do not forgive surprises.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a promise to fix on site in exchange for keeping the vessel booking. The control is a purchase-order term that makes shipment release conditional on a passed, witnessed factory test, with payment against shipping documents tied to that release.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a failed test as bad news to be hidden or argued away. It is good news delivered early.

Callback

Last week, Bram's room taught you to split a bundled request and give a dated answer. Here the bundle is the defect and the vessel booking: split them, solve the defect first, then solve the shipping with the time the float allows.

Recap

Thank the supplier for a real test. Ask for the cause and a retest at the works. Check the float before reacting to the vessel. Keep payment tied to a passed test. Put the decision in writing the same day.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: the week's six questions on procurement, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Shipment release is conditional on a passed, witnessed factory test.
Payment against shipping documents is tied to that release.
I ask for the cause of any failure before discussing shipping.
I check remaining float before reacting to a vessel booking.
My engineer gives the technical facts; I set the conditions.
Any agreement to ship with an open defect is secured by retention, warranty and a replacement commitment.
The decision and the effect on float are confirmed in writing the same day.
head: Field checklist
speak: A chiller has failed its witnessed performance test: about 8 percent short on cooling and below its guaranteed efficiency. The supplier wants to ship and fix it on site to keep the vessel booking. I thank them for a real test, then ask what exactly will change and whether they can make that change and retest at the works this week. Then I stay quiet and watch the factory engineer. Before reacting to the vessel, I check the register: the item still has about 7 weeks of float, so missing one sailing costs float but not the finish date, while shipping a defective unit could mean a 30-week replacement. Payment against shipping documents stays tied to a passed test, which keeps the factory motivated. If anyone proposes shipping with an open defect, I ask for retention, an extended warranty and a replacement commitment. And the decision goes in writing the same day.
terms: Performance test — a test proving that equipment delivers its specified output and efficiency under defined conditions.
Shipment release — the buyer's written permission for goods to leave the factory, often tied to inspection or testing.
Retention — part of the price held back until defined performance or completion conditions are met.

hostile.q: Your refusal to ship has cost us the vessel. Why should we absorb three weeks for a calibration fix?
hostile.a: Because the unit did not meet its specification at your works, and the purchase order ties shipment to a passed test. If it is calibration, a retest this week proves it and we ship on the next vessel, which our float can absorb. I would rather lose a sailing than install a unit that may need replacing. Let us agree the retest date now.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 115 Review: Long Leads, Landed Cost and the Border
summary: Six questions test the week: need dates, factory acceptance tests, the switchgear failure, landed cost, Incoterms and recovering float. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical purchase order, and the boardroom drill explains procurement in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: an item is not delivered until it is on site, cleared, certified and accepted, so procurement is planned backward from the need date, priced on landed cost, and controlled by tests and terms that hold the supplier to acceptance, not shipment.

Recall

Q. What should a purchase order say about shipment release?

A. That shipment is released only after a passed, witnessed factory acceptance test, with payment against shipping documents tied to that release.

Q. What is the root cause in most procurement failures?

A. Treating procurement as buying a price rather than delivering an accepted item to a need date, with no single owner for the whole chain.

Q. What is an approved fabricator?

A. A fabricator recognised by the building official, often through a certification program, whose shop work may be accepted without separate special inspection.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions without notes, you can read a procurement plan, a supplier's quote and a purchase order and see where the schedule and the money are exposed. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is a need date, and why does procurement start from it?

Answer: The latest date an item can arrive without delaying the critical path. It is fixed by the schedule, so every step of the chain is scheduled backward from it to find the date you must start.

Question 2. What does a factory acceptance test protect against?

Answer: Shipping equipment that does not meet its specification or certification. A fault fixed at the works costs days; the same fault found on site can cost months and a return shipment.

Question 3. In the switchgear case, what was the root cause?

Answer: Treating procurement as buying a price, with no owner for the chain from design to the inspector's acceptance. The equipment lacked the required certification and stalled at customs.

Question 4. Name five items that make up landed cost besides the quoted price.

Answer: Any five of export packing, freight, cargo insurance, customs duty, import value-added or goods and services tax, brokerage, port charges, inland transport, storage, currency movement and the cost of early payment.

Question 5. What do Incoterms 2020 decide, and what do they not decide?

Answer: They decide who pays each leg, who bears risk and where, and who clears export and import. They do not decide when title passes; the sales contract and governing law do.

Question 6. When an item's float runs out, how do you choose a recovery?

Answer: Price each option, such as faster freight, pre-clearance, faster reviews or resequencing, against the cost of a critical-path week, and prefer the cheapest that restores float.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Quincy built the long-lead register and scheduled from the need date. Ford and Cole took a composite case of switchgear that cleared customs late and failed inspection, giving Rule 115. Nadia built landed cost and priced currency and early payment. Devika taught Incoterms, classification, value and origin, and compared Canada and Guyana. Quincy computed float on a chiller chain and priced recovery options. Quincy then ran the call where a factory test failed and the supplier wanted to ship.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical purchase order extract and find the defects before reading on.

Purchase Order 22. Equipment: main switchgear to manufacturer's standard. Delivery: FOB, as soon as possible. Price: 900,000, payable 50 percent on order and 50 percent on shipment. Testing: manufacturer's certificate to accompany the goods. Title: passes on delivery. Customs: buyer to arrange. Certification: as per manufacturer's country.

The defects. First, manufacturer's standard is not a specification, so nothing ties the equipment to the design. Second, FOB is a sea-only term and names no port; the place must be precise, and a term for any mode of transport may fit better for packaged equipment. Third, as soon as possible is not a date; the purchase order needs a delivery date derived from the need date. Fourth, the price has no currency, which leaves the exchange-rate exposure undefined. Fifth, half the price on order is unsecured and half on shipment is due whether or not the goods work; payment should be tied to a passed witnessed test and secured by a bond. Sixth, a manufacturer's certificate is not a witnessed factory acceptance test. Seventh, certification as per the manufacturer's country ignores the authority having jurisdiction, which is exactly the switchgear failure. Eighth, title on delivery while half the price is paid on order means paying for goods you do not own; and customs to be arranged by the buyer with no broker or classification named leaves the declaration risk unmanaged.

The corrected order, in outline

A corrected version, still hypothetical, would name the specification section and drawings, require the certification mark the local authority accepts, state an Incoterms 2020 rule with a precise named place and the insurance cover, give a delivery date tied to the need date, state the currency, tie payments to a witnessed test and secure any advance with a bond, pass title on payment against marked goods, and name the customs broker and the agreed classification. Every correction adds a document, a date or a named person.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week to a board in two minutes, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Our opening date is decided by a handful of items that take most of a year to make: switchgear, generators, elevators, chillers and the facade. We keep a register of them, scheduled backward from the latest date each can arrive, and we bought the longest ones early, before the main contract. We compare suppliers on landed cost, including freight, duty, import tax, currency and early payment, not on the quoted price. Our purchase orders state the trade term and place, the insurance, the currency and when title passes, and our customs broker confirms classification before anything ships. Nothing ships until it passes a witnessed factory test, and payment follows the test. Each item's float is reported weekly, and when float runs low we price recovery against what a week of delay costs us."

Score yourself: did you lead with the opening date, name the need date and landed cost, and tie payment to testing? If not, record it again tomorrow.

One more test of understanding

Kema adds a short practical exercise. Take any building you know and name the three items you believe would decide its opening date if they were late. For each, guess the factory lead time, then ask a supplier or a contractor for the real figure. Most people underestimate electrical equipment and elevators and overestimate finishes. The gap between your guess and the real figure is the size of the blind spot this week was designed to close.

Linking the week to the next one

Next week is quality. Notice how much of this week was already quality work: the witnessed factory test, the certification mark, the submittal that should have been rejected. Procurement decides what arrives; quality decides whether what arrives, and what is built from it, is accepted. The two systems share the same backbone of named owners, dated steps and written records.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a purchase order that defines delivery as shipment. The control is to define delivery as acceptance in the purchase order, the register and the payment terms.

The beginner's mistake

Letting the contractor's buyer choose the trade term and the supplier on price alone, without seeing the landed-cost sheet or the certification requirement.

Callback

In Week 52, Marco taught delivery methods and buyout. Early owner purchase of long-lead equipment is a buyout decision taken before the builder exists, and it must be written so the order can be assigned cleanly to the contractor when it is appointed, with warranties and responsibilities intact.

Recap

Schedule from the need date. Price on landed cost. Choose the trade term deliberately and state title separately. Confirm classification with a broker. Test before shipping. Watch float weekly. Rule 115: an item is not delivered until it is accepted.

Next: Ingrid on First Principles: the quality plan, inspection and test plans, and the hold points that protect the work.

What a witnessed factory acceptance test protects against.
The switchgear failure and Rule 115.
The parts of landed cost.
What Incoterms 2020 decide and do not decide.
How to price recovery when float runs out.
head: The six questions
speak: This week, procurement. A handful of long-lead items, like switchgear, generators, elevators, chillers and facade, decide the opening date. I keep them on one register, scheduled backward from each need date, and I buy the longest ones early if the contractor is not yet appointed. I compare suppliers on landed cost, adding freight, insurance, duty, import tax, brokerage, port and inland charges, currency risk and the cost of paying early. My purchase orders name an Incoterms 2020 rule and a precise place, the insurance cover, the currency and when title passes, because Incoterms do not settle title. A licensed customs broker confirms classification, value and origin. Nothing ships until it passes a witnessed factory test, and payment follows the test. I watch every item's float weekly and price recovery against a week of delay. Rule 115: an item is delivered only when it is on site, cleared, certified and accepted.
terms: Early owner package — equipment bought directly by the owner before the main contractor is appointed, later assigned to it.
Assignment — transfer of a contract's rights, and sometimes obligations, from one party to another.
Named place — the precise location stated with an Incoterms rule, where delivery or risk transfer occurs.

hostile.q: Your purchase order says delivery is FOB as soon as possible. What date are you holding the supplier to?
hostile.a: None, which is the defect, and it is being corrected. The revised order states a delivery date derived from the need date on our register, names the Incoterms rule and the precise place, ties shipment release to a witnessed factory test, and links payment to that release. I will send it for signature this week.
